label: The Jacobian Equation
notes: Welcome to the chapter that turns a transport map into a differential equation. Mass conservation, written infinitesimally, forces the source density to equal the target density at the image point times the absolute Jacobian determinant. That single identity is the bridge from couplings to partial differential equations and, ultimately, to regularity theory.

label: Push-Forward and Mass Conservation
notes: Recall the push-forward condition. A map T transports mu onto nu when the mass of every target set equals the mass of its preimage. We rewrite this integral identity through a change of variables, which is exactly where the Jacobian determinant of T enters and where the chapter's central equation will be born.

label: Change of Variables
notes: The classical change-of-variables formula is the engine here. For a smooth injective map with positive Jacobian, integrating against the target density and substituting y equals T of x produces a factor of the Jacobian determinant. Demanding that this reproduces the source density pointwise gives the Jacobian equation directly.

label: The Jacobian Equation
notes: Here is the heart of the chapter, stated cleanly. The source density at x equals the target density at the image times the absolute value of the determinant of the differential of T. Emphasise that the determinant carries an absolute value because mass is unsigned, and that the identity is required only mu-almost-everywhere.

label: Local Mass Balance
notes: Walk the audience through the picture. A tiny volume element around x is mapped to a parallelepiped around T of x whose volume is scaled by the absolute Jacobian determinant. Equal mass in both cells forces density times volume to balance, which is the Jacobian equation read geometrically rather than analytically.

label: Quadratic Cost: T = grad psi
notes: For the quadratic cost, Brenier's theorem says the optimal map is the gradient of a convex potential psi. Substitute T equal to grad psi into the Jacobian equation. The differential of the map becomes the Hessian of psi, so its determinant is the Monge-Ampere operator acting on a convex function.

label: The Monge-Ampere Equation
notes: This slide states the specialization explicitly. The determinant of the Hessian of psi equals the source density divided by the target density evaluated at grad psi. This fully nonlinear second-order equation, of Monge-Ampere type, is the analytic form the transport problem takes for quadratic cost.

label: Approximate Differentiability
notes: Optimal maps need not be smooth, so the classical Jacobian may not exist everywhere. The fix is approximate differentiability: at almost every point the map admits a linear approximation in the measure-theoretic density sense. Brenier maps, being gradients of convex functions, are differentiable Lebesgue-almost-everywhere by Aleksandrov's theorem.

label: Aleksandrov Second Derivatives
notes: Aleksandrov's theorem guarantees that a convex function has a second-order Taylor expansion almost everywhere, defining the Aleksandrov Hessian. This pointwise Hessian, rather than any distributional object, is the determinant that appears in the Jacobian equation. Distinguish it carefully from the larger distributional Monge-Ampere measure.

label: Where the Identity Holds
notes: Collect the technical caveats. The Jacobian equation holds mu-almost-everywhere using the approximate Jacobian, provided the densities are honest and the map is the optimal one. Stress that almost-everywhere is the natural and unavoidable register here, and that injectivity up to null sets is what makes the substitution legitimate.

label: The Bridge to PDE
notes: Close by naming the payoff. The Jacobian equation converts a measure-coupling problem into a determinant equation, and for quadratic cost into Monge-Ampere. That equation is the gateway to Caffarelli's and later regularity theory, and it reappears whenever volume distortion of optimal maps must be quantified, as in curvature bounds.
